Pan American Airways,
New York City.
Dear Bix:
Damaris and I have read and re-read your letter a number
for the fact itself, and for the news communicated in it.
We had a letter from Mrs. Peck yesterday afternoon in
which she says she plans to leave San Francisco for Miami on
December 15 or 16. We are hoping that she will remain with us
this time until her return to China is sanctioned by the Depart-
ment of state.
When that will be, wo pu tung! We wonder whether
Bonå, in expressing the opinion that the major trouble will be
in sixty days, was not prompted more by hope than by actual
conviction; not that we for a moment question his judgement, but
we have observed a conspicuous absence in Mr. Peck's recent
letters of any indication as to what thoughts in the premises are
entertained in official cireles. It is quite possible -- and
also probable -- that his letters are drafted with the thought
that they might fall into unauthorized hands in transit.
being the case, and knowing Mr. Peck's discretion, we attempt in
each case to read into his letters many unrecorded remarks and
opinions. Nevertheless, none of us is confident that Mrs. Peck
will be able to return to the Orient -- to China, at least -- in
the immediate future.
Looking at the matter selfishly, we may be
prejudiced as we are adding another bedroom and bath to our house
primarily for the purpose of making Mrs. Peck comfortable for a
long stay.
Bond's graphic account of recent CNAC operations would seem
entirely uncredible had we not lived in China and known the
personnel concerned. In one of his recent letters to us, Mr.
Peck repeated in detail Bond's description to him of the
landing of the Commodore at Ichang.
He said that the co-pilot
hung far out of the cockpit and endeavored to illuminate the
landing area with a weak flashlight as they approached for the

long experience should meet with
the disaster that was the fate

aviation report up to date.
Out of deference to the rather
delicate relations of my former colleagues, particularly as
regards the transmitting of military information through ordinary

-2-
mail channels, I have not asked them to make an attempt to keep
me posted.
This leaves to me, then, only Ies Lewis, Patterson,
Fuzzy Vaughn (Socony) and a few other businessmen as sources of
information.
They of course have their hands about full without
taking on the additional burden of trying to satisfy my
curiosity.
I occasionally get an interesting tid bit from one or
two of my
British friends in the RAFA at Shanghai and Hong Kong.
Since all this information is at best sketchy,
and in most cases
without confirmation, I have about concluded that I wouldn't
accomplish anything useful by attempting to revise my report on
the basis and strength of it.
I would, however, like very much
to have a look at the information you refer to in your letter. I
understand fully its confidential nature and I would you may be
sure treat it accordingly il, under the above circumstances you
would still wish to send it along to me.
I haven't found it
possible, by the way.
to reconcile the figure of 750 planes said
to have been available in China at the outbreak of the present
trouble.
At the time I left for home (November 1936) there were
supposed to be about 400 planes (I quote from memory, as my
census is up at the ollice) ineluding the breguets, boenings,
Falke-Wolfes, etc. Adding to this figure the number of planes
imported into China (and Hong Kong), as reported by_the U.s.
Department of Commerce in its commercial releases, I can get a
total of not more than about 550. Of course I may have missed
some D of C reports,
and of course there doubtless have been a
number oi importations from Europe, Russia etc. Nevertheless, as
you remark, the number-one's certainly appear to have seized upon
an optimistic conclusion without any regard to the facts insofar
as the air force is concerned.
I am enclosing herewith two copies of the Art Lym story
that was included in my report.
The pertinent facts came direct
fron Art himself.
The temptation to embellish them with a spot
or two of imagination and exageration was too great to resist,
however, and it may well be that I treated the matter a little
facetiously.
I noted the other day that Art's picture which
appeared in
the report made a first-class liar of me. The
picture shows him not wearing goggles, whereas my story turned
on the fact that he was blinded by tears when he removed his
goggles. I now conclude that I'll have to tell the truth hereafter,
or commercialize on the distortion of fact as has been done so well
recently by a mutual friend.
Incidentally,
I am sure you would be
interested in Bill Grooch's
"Winged Highways" which was recently
published, if you haven't already seen it. Bill Ehmer, too, has
broken out with commercial verbage.
A story over his nane,
"Ex Mechanic"
called, I believe, ALr Trati, recent issue of a pulp magazine
In this turn of events, I shoul
think you would feel delinquent in not having a few books to your
credit by this time.
Grooch referred to Rumill and Gast in his
book as a couple of
barnstorming co-pilots or the like. Rumill was
over
the other evening, and in the privacy of our home gave free
vent to his wrath. His comment totalled: "I'd like to see that
fellow. I'd sure tell him a thing or two. Gosh!"
That is real
vehemence, coming from Rumill, 11 you will recall his usual
tendeney to say not more than two or at most three words in
succession.
dorolt
SIPOS

-3-
Thanksgiving this year fell on the fifth anniversary of the
Seeshan interlude.
In token of the special occasion for real
giving of thanks, we had the rummils over for dinner.
While the
fact was not mentioned by either of us, I am sure at
• least two
silent toasts were drunk to you on
that occasion. I am sure I
have remarked to you many times that that experience was one I
wouldn't take a pot of gold for; but at the same time, one I
wouldn't willing repeat for the same amount. We all - that is
Damaris, the Pecks, and I - look back on it now pleasantly as
gratefully. The Pecks have a delightful and enviable
faculty of recalling all the enjoyable aspects and circumstances
of things which have happened in the past.
Much of this has been
imparted to me.
Accordingly,
the Seeshan
affair seems now more
than ever belore the greatest and most impressive of all the
unusual near-tragic, but comic, things that have come our way.
Viewed from my side of the association, I praise the day I
decided to make a bid for a connection with Pan American. While
Consular work was pleasant and extremely interesting, and
although my associates, both superior and subordinate, left
nothing to be asked for, my decision to change would be unaltered
if I had it to do over again.
You will probably recall that I
was pretty enthusiastic about aviation before I came with the
Company•
I was perhaps a little fanatically so. Analizing my
present feelings on the subject, I think that in all probability
I am just as interested and enthusiastic, but that my interest
and enthusiasm are "growing up". At any
rate, I hope so, for I
am confident that il I can retain their force
and then direct
that force along the correct channels, a worthwhile dividend will
accrue. In a few more days I will have completed my second year
with the Company, and viewing my present assignment in the light
of what I have learned during that time, I fully realize how
very fortunate I am.
In the first place, Mr. Snyder lacks nothing
as an immediate chief.
This is of course apart from our relations
the office.
Damaris and I have come to know Mrs. Snyder
and him. Knowing as you do, the people we left behind in China,
I am sure you will understand what I wish to say when I remark
that the Snyders measure up in all respects.
Your comment respecting the Pecks coincides in every way the
extra-family leeling I hold for them.
The respect and regard you
entertain for the Pecks is fully reciprocated, I can assure you
on unimpeachable authority, and I know also that they both hold a
real affection for "the Bixbys".
To speak in my own behalf on
this score would be merely superfluous!
I apologize for having gone to such lengths with this.
I am
well aware of the demands made on your time by the duties
Division "sponsor", I do not therefore,
expect that you will be
able (or wish) to give this more than a hasty perusal; similarly,
we 11 look forward to your next letter,
but will not expect it
until it turns up in the mail some morning.
Our very best regards to you all.
Very sincerely,
wensures,
